hints: `Select` is deferred: it runs when the query is enumerated.
By the time `Sum` runs, the list holds four numbers.
exercises.solution: `q` is a recipe, not a result. `Sum` enumerates it after 4 has been added, so it computes 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 = **100**. Had the code written `list.Select(x => x * 10).ToList()`, the answer would be 60.

feedback.message: Not yet — that is the second line. In a `for` loop there is one variable `i` for the whole loop. What is its value when the lambdas finally run?
Not yet — the loop stops when `i < 3` is false. What value makes it false?

hints: A `for` loop declares its variable once; `foreach` declares a fresh one for each pass (since C# 5).
exercises.solution: All three lambdas capture the *same* variable `i`, and they run after the loop has finished, when `i` is 3. So the first line is `3,3,3`. A `foreach` loop gets a fresh variable on each pass (a deliberate change in C# 5), so the second line is `0,1,2`. To fix the `for` version, copy the variable inside the loop: `int copy = i; actions.Add(() => copy);`.

hints: Group the words by their first letter.
Which letter starts the most words?
exercises.solution: The groups are `a` (apple, avocado, apricot), `b` (banana, blueberry) and `c` (cherry). Ordered by size, the largest is `a` with 3 words, so the program prints `a 3`.

hints: Keep the multiples of 3, then square them.
exercises.solution: The query is `Enumerable.Range(1, 10).Where(n => n % 3 == 0).Select(n => n * n)`. The multiples of 3 up to 10 are 3, 6 and 9, whose squares are `9 36 81`.


feedback.message: Not yet — that would be the sum. Follow the lambda: the accumulator is multiplied by 10 each time.

hints: Without a seed, `Aggregate` starts with the first item as the accumulator.
Then it applies the lambda with each following item: 1 → 12 → ...
exercises.solution: `Aggregate` folds the sequence from the left: start with 1; then 1×10+2 = 12; then 12×10+3 = 123; then 123×10+4 = **1234**. `Sum`, `Max` and friends are special cases of this fold.

exercises.prompt: `int[] readings` may be empty or may contain no reading above the alarm level. You write `int first = readings.Where(r => r > alarm).FirstOrDefault();`. What is the risk?

options.label: It throws InvalidOperationException when nothing matches
options.feedback: Not yet — that is what `First` does. `FirstOrDefault` returns a default value instead.

options.label: When nothing matches it returns 0, which the rest of the code may mistake for a real reading of 0
options.feedback: Yes. The default of `int` is 0, indistinguishable from a genuine 0. Use `Any` first, the overload `FirstOrDefault(-1)` with an impossible value, or work with `int?`.

options.label: It enumerates the array twice
options.feedback: Not yet — `FirstOrDefault` stops at the first match; the query is enumerated once.

options.label: It returns null, which causes a NullReferenceException
options.feedback: Not yet — `int` is a value type and cannot be null; the default is 0.

hints: Can the caller tell "no match" from "matched a 0"?
exercises.solution: `FirstOrDefault` returns `default(int)`, which is 0, when nothing matches, and a caller cannot distinguish that from a real reading of 0. Make the absence explicit: test with `Any`, pass an explicit default (`FirstOrDefault(r => r > alarm, -1)`, available since .NET 6), or project to `int?` so that no match is `null`.

exercises.prompt: With Entity Framework Core, `db.Orders` is an `IQueryable` over a table of ten million orders. Which query downloads the whole table into memory?

options.label: `db.Orders.Where(o => o.Total > 1000).ToList()`
options.feedback: Not yet — the `Where` is part of the `IQueryable` query, so it becomes a SQL `WHERE` and only matching rows are sent.

options.label: `db.Orders.AsEnumerable().Where(o => o.Total > 1000).ToList()`
options.feedback: Yes. `AsEnumerable()` switches to LINQ to Objects, so the `Where` runs in your process on every row the database sends: all ten million.

options.label: `db.Orders.Count(o => o.Total > 1000)`
options.feedback: Not yet — this becomes `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE ...`, returning a single number.

options.label: `db.Orders.OrderBy(o => o.Total).Take(10).ToList()`
options.feedback: Not yet — ordering and `Take` translate to SQL (`ORDER BY` and a row limit), so only ten rows come back.

hints: Operators on an `IQueryable` are translated to SQL; operators on an `IEnumerable` run in memory.
Which call changes the type of the sequence from `IQueryable` to `IEnumerable`?
exercises.solution: In (b), `AsEnumerable()` ends the translatable part of the query, so EF Core sends `SELECT * FROM Orders` and the filter runs in memory over every row. In (a), (c) and (d) every operator is applied to the `IQueryable` and translated into SQL, so the database does the filtering, counting, ordering and limiting.
